title: Milestone Project 4: Data Logger and Report Writer
text:
🏁 Milestone Project 4: Data Logger and Report Writer
In this milestone project, you will build a complete scientific data logging pipeline: 1. Acquisition / Simulation: Generate a time series of thermal cooling data according to Newton’s Law of Cooling with simulated sensor noise. 2. File Export: Format the data into clean, aligned columns and write it to a text data log (cooling_log.dat) with metadata headers. 3. File Ingestion: Read the data file back into memory using line parsing and NumPy. 4. Analysis & Visualization: Compute statistical summary metrics and render a diagnostic plot with error bounds, saving the resulting graph to disk.

title: Milestone Project 4: Data Logger and Report Writer
text:
Complete Project Code: thermal_logger.py
Create a new file in Spyder named thermal_logger.py and run it:
"""
thermal_logger.py
=================
Milestone Project 4: Generates data, writes a formatted log file,
reads it back, and plots a verification figure.
"""

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def generate_and_log_data(filename="cooling_log.dat"):
    """
    Simulates thermal cooling: T(t) = T_env + (T0 - T_env) * exp(-r * t)
    and logs the formatted data to a file.
    """
    print("\n1. Generating thermal cooling dataset...")
    
    # Physics parameters
    t_env = 22.0     # Ambient temperature in Celsius
    t_0 = 95.0       # Initial temperature (boiling liquid)
    r = 0.045        # Cooling rate constant (1/s)
    
    # Time points from 0 to 120 seconds
    time_pts = np.linspace(0, 120, 41)  # Every 3 seconds
    
    # Theoretical temperature decay
    t_clean = t_env + (t_0 - t_env) * np.exp(-r * time_pts)
    
    # Add sensor noise (+/- 0.6 °C)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=2026)
    sensor_noise = rng.normal(0.0, 0.6, size=len(time_pts))
    t_measured = t_clean + sensor_noise
    
    # Write formatted file
    print(f"2. Writing formatted log to '{filename}'...")
    with open(filename, "w") as f:
        # File Header and Metadata
        f.write("# =========================================================\n")
        f.write("# EXPERIMENTAL DATA LOG: Newton's Law of Cooling\n")
        f.write("# Environment: 22.0 C | Initial Temp: 95.0 C | Rate: 0.045 /s\n")
        f.write("# =========================================================\n")
        f.write(f"{'Index':<6} | {'Time (s)':>10} | {'Theory (C)':>12} | {'Sensor (C)':>12}\n")
        f.write("# " + "-" * 50 + "\n")
        
        # Data Rows
        for i, (t_val, clean_val, meas_val) in enumerate(zip(time_pts, t_clean, t_measured), start=1):
            f.write(f"{i:<6d} | {t_val:10.2f} | {clean_val:12.3f} | {meas_val:12.3f}\n")
            
    print(f">> File '{filename}' successfully written ({len(time_pts)} records).")


def read_and_plot_data(filename="cooling_log.dat"):
    """
    Reads the formatted text file back from disk and plots the results.
    """
    print(f"\n3. Reading data back from '{filename}'...")
    
    times = []
    theory = []
    sensor = []
    
    with open(filename, "r") as f:
        for line in f:
            # Skip comment and header lines starting with '#'
            if line.startswith("#") or "Time" in line or not line.strip():
                continue
            
            # Split row by the '|' delimiter
            parts = line.strip().split("|")
            if len(parts) == 4:
                idx = int(parts[0])
                t_val = float(parts[1])
                theo_val = float(parts[2])
                sens_val = float(parts[3])
                
                times.append(t_val)
                theory.append(theo_val)
                sensor.append(sens_val)
                
    times = np.array(times)
    theory = np.array(theory)
    sensor = np.array(sensor)
    
    print(f"Parsed {len(times)} records. Generating report plot...")
    
    # 4. Plot and Save
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 7), sharex=True, 
                                   gridspec_kw={'height_ratios': [3, 1]})
    
    # Top Panel: Cooling Curves
    ax1.plot(times, theory, "b-", linewidth=2, label="Theoretical Model")
    ax1.scatter(times, sensor, color="red", marker="o", s=30, label="Thermocouple Sensor", zorder=3)
    ax1.axhline(22.0, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="Ambient Temp (22 °C)")
    ax1.set(title="Liquid Thermal Cooling Profile", ylabel="Temperature (°C)")
    ax1.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
    ax1.legend()
    
    # Bottom Panel: Residual Sensor Error
    residuals = sensor - theory
    ax2.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax2.stem(times, residuals, linefmt="k:", markerfmt="ro", basefmt="k-")
    ax2.set(title="Sensor Residual Errors", xlabel="Time (seconds)", ylabel="Error (°C)", ylim=(-2.5, 2.5))
    ax2.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
    
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("cooling_report.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    print(">> Report plot saved to 'cooling_report.png'!")
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    generate_and_log_data()
    read_and_plot_data()
When you run this script: 1. cooling_log.dat is created on disk with formatted headers and columns. 2. The file is opened, parsed, and checked for accuracy. 3. cooling_report.png is generated, showing the thermal decay curve and the residual sensor noise below it.

title: Testing and Debugging
text:
Chapter 12: Testing and Debugging
In scientific research, buggy code is dangerous. It doesn’t just crash your computer—it can produce plausible-looking but subtly incorrect calculations, invalidating an entire semester of lab work.
This chapter teaches you systematic strategies for testing your functions and using Spyder’s visual debugger to locate and fix bugs with confidence.

title: Testing and Debugging
text:
12.1 Black-Box vs Glass-Box Testing
When verifying a function, there are two distinct perspectives:
  Black-Box Testing:
  Input (X) ──► [ ??? Unknown Interior ??? ] ──► Output (Y)
  (Test against the specification without looking at the internal code)

  Glass-Box (White-Box) Testing:
  Input (X) ──► [ if condition -> loop -> return ] ──► Output (Y)
  (Design tests to exercise every internal branch, loop, and path in the code)

Black-Box Testing: You test the function based solely on its docstring and specifications. It tests whether the software delivers what the user expects.
Glass-Box Testing: You inspect the code lines directly and choose inputs specifically designed to trigger every if, elif, and else branch, and to test loops with zero, one, and multiple iterations.

title: Testing and Debugging
section: 12.2 Designing Test Cases: Typical, Edge, and Boundary Values
text:
12.2 Designing Test Cases: Typical, Edge, and Boundary Values
A good scientist does not test a function with just one random number. Always test three categories of inputs:
                  Input Domain: e.g. Speed v in [0, 100] m/s
       +-----------------------------------------------------------+
       |   0                10              50              99 100 |
       +-----------------------------------------------------------+
           ▲                                ▲                    ▲
           └── Boundary (Zero)              └── Typical (Middle) └── Boundary (Max)

Typical Cases: Normal expected values (e.g., \(v = 25.0\)).
Boundary Cases: Values right at the limits of validity (e.g., \(v = 0.0\) or \(v = 100.0\)).
Edge / Extreme Cases: Empty inputs ([]), single-element collections, negative numbers where positives are expected, or very large floats (\(10^{15}\)).


Runnable Example: Testing a Velocity Calculator
def average_velocity(distance, time):
    """Computes v = d / t. Distance >= 0, Time > 0."""
    if time <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Time must be strictly positive!")
    if distance < 0:
        raise ValueError("Distance cannot be negative!")
    return distance / time

# Formal test suite
def test_average_velocity():
    # 1. Typical case
    assert average_velocity(100.0, 5.0) == 20.0, "Failed typical case"
    
    # 2. Boundary: Zero distance
    assert average_velocity(0.0, 5.0) == 0.0, "Failed zero distance boundary"
    
    # 3. Boundary: Small time step
    assert abs(average_velocity(1.0, 0.01) - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Failed small time case"
    
    # 4. Edge cases: Expecting exceptions
    try:
        average_velocity(50.0, 0.0)
        print("ERROR: Zero time should have raised ValueError!")
    except ValueError:
        pass  # Expected behavior!

    print("All test cases passed successfully!")

test_average_velocity()

title: Testing and Debugging
text:
12.3 Types of Bugs
Understanding the nature of a bug determines how you hunt it down:








Bug Category
Characteristics
How to Catch It




Overt
Obvious crash with an explicit Python error (e.g. ZeroDivisionError).
Read the traceback line number.


Covert (Silent)
The code runs without error but outputs incorrect physics numbers.
Unit tests and assertion checks.


Persistent
Occurs every single time you run the script with the same inputs.
Reproduce it in Spyder with a breakpoint.


Intermittent
Occurs unpredictably (often caused by unseeded random numbers or file race conditions).
Fix random seeds (seed=42) to make it persistent.

title: Testing and Debugging
text:
12.4 Hypothesis-and-Confirmation Debugging
Do not change lines of code at random hoping the bug disappears! Follow the scientific method:
  1. Observe the failure: "Output is negative (-5.4), but energy must be >= 0."
  2. Formulate a hypothesis: "Perhaps velocity was subtracted instead of added."
  3. Design an experiment: Insert a print statement or check the Variable Explorer.
  4. Confirm or reject: Check whether the intermediate variable matches expectation.

12.6 Debugging a Recursive Function Step by Step
Let us debug a recursive countdown function to see the call stack in action:
def countdown(n):
    print(f"Entering countdown(n={n})")
    if n == 0:
        print("Blast off! (Base case reached)")
        return
    countdown(n - 1)
    print(f"Exiting countdown(n={n})")

countdown(3)
Output Trace:
Entering countdown(n=3)
Entering countdown(n=2)
Entering countdown(n=1)
Entering countdown(n=0)
Blast off! (Base case reached)

Exiting countdown(n=2)

Notice how the frames unwind in reverse order from the stack! If you omit the base case if n == 0, Python recursively calls until hitting RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded.

text:
Chapter 13: Exceptions
When an unexpected event occurs during program execution—such as trying to divide by zero, reading a missing file, or parsing text where a number was expected—Python creates an Exception.
If your program does not handle the exception, it halts immediately with an error message (crashes). With exception handling, your programs can anticipate errors, recover gracefully, and continue executing.

text:
13.2 The try–except Block
The fundamental construct for handling errors:
try:
    # Risky code that might fail
    resistance = float(input("Enter resistance (Ohms): "))
    current = 12.0 / resistance
    print(f"Current is: {current:.2f} A")
except:
    print("An error occurred during calculation!")

College Tip: Avoid bare except:. It catches everything, including user interruptions (Ctrl+C) and typos! Always catch specific exceptions.

title: Exceptions
text:
13.3 Handling Specific Exceptions & Multiple Clauses
You can chain multiple except blocks to handle different failure modes appropriately:

Runnable Example
def safe_sensor_parser(raw_string, default_val=0.0):
    """Parses a numerical sensor string, returning default_val if corrupted."""
    try:
        clean_text = raw_string.strip()
        reading = float(clean_text)
        return reading
    except ValueError:
        print(f"Warning: Corrupted text '{raw_string}' could not be converted to float.")
        return default_val
    except AttributeError:
        print(f"Warning: Expected string input, but received type {type(raw_string)}.")
        return default_val

# Testing different inputs
print("Test 1 (Valid):    ", safe_sensor_parser("  24.85  "))
print("Test 2 (Corrupt):  ", safe_sensor_parser("N/A_SENSOR_TIMEOUT"))
print("Test 3 (Wrong type):", safe_sensor_parser(None))

title: Exceptions
text:
13.4 else and finally Clauses
The complete structure includes else and finally:
  try:
      # Risky action (e.g. open file, read data)
  except FileNotFoundError:
      # Executes ONLY if FileNotFoundError happens
  else:
      # Executes ONLY if NO exception was raised!
  finally:
      # ALWAYS executes, whether an error occurred or not!
      # (Ideal for closing hardware connections or cleanup)

Runnable Example
def process_data_file(filename):
    file = None
    try:
        print(f"\nAttempting to open '{filename}'...")
        file = open(filename, "r")
        content = file.read()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: File '{filename}' was not found on disk.")
    else:
        print("Success! File read without issues.")
        print(f"Total characters: {len(content)}")
    finally:
        if file is not None and not file.closed:
            file.close()
            print("Cleanup: File object closed safely.")
        print("Done with file operation attempt.")

# Test with non-existent file
process_data_file("non_existent_lab_reading.txt")

🏁 Capstone Project: Robust Data Analysis Pipeline
Congratulations on making it to the Capstone Project! In this comprehensive project, you will unite everything you have learned throughout this book into an industrial-grade, robust scientific data pipeline.

title: Capstone Project: Robust Data Analysis Pipeline
text:
1. Pipeline Architecture
The pipeline consists of four modular functions designed for clean separation of concerns: 1. generate_mock_laboratory_file(filename) — Generates a realistic CSV file with headers, comments, valid sensor data, and corrupted values. 2. load_and_clean_data(filename) — Opens the file, applies defensive exception handling to discard corrupted rows, and returns clean NumPy arrays. 3. analyze_spectrum(wavelengths, intensities) — Performs numerical baseline removal, smooths signal noise, locates emission peaks, and calculates total energy. 4. generate_visual_and_text_report(...) — Renders the multi-panel figure and writes a formatted executive summary file.

title: Capstone Project: Robust Data Analysis Pipeline
text:
2. Complete Pipeline Implementation: pipeline_capstone.py
Create a file named pipeline_capstone.py in your Spyder editor and run it (F5):
"""
pipeline_capstone.py
====================
Capstone Project: An end-to-end robust scientific analysis pipeline
incorporating File I/O, Exception Handling, NumPy, and Matplotlib.
"""

import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def generate_mock_laboratory_file(filename="spectrometry_raw.csv"):
    """Generates mock optical emission spectrometry data with corrupted rows."""
    print(f"[Stage 1] Generating raw laboratory file: '{filename}'...")
    
    # 200 wavelength points from 400 nm to 700 nm (visible light spectrum)
    wavelengths = np.linspace(400.0, 700.0, 201)
    
    # Emission peaks at 480nm (Hydrogen-beta) and 656nm (Hydrogen-alpha)
    peak1 = 35.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((wavelengths - 486.1) / 8.0)**2)
    peak2 = 80.0 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((wavelengths - 656.3) / 10.0)**2)
    baseline = 15.0 + 0.02 * wavelengths
    
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=2026)
    noise = rng.normal(0, 1.5, size=len(wavelengths))
    intensity = baseline + peak1 + peak2 + noise
    
    with open(filename, "w") as f:
        f.write("# OPTICAL EMISSION SPECTROMETER LAB RUN 42\n")
        f.write("# Instrument: OceanOptics-HR2000 | Operator: College Lab Team\n")
        f.write("Wavelength(nm),Intensity(counts)\n")
        
        for i, (w, intens) in enumerate(zip(wavelengths, intensity)):
            # Introduce intentional realistic data corruption at isolated indices
            if i == 45:
                f.write("467.50,SENSOR_COMM_TIMEOUT\n")  # Corrupted float
            elif i == 110:
                f.write("CORRUPTED_LINE_DROPPED_SYNC\n")   # Missing column
            elif i == 160:
                f.write("640.00,-9999.00\n")             # Out-of-bounds error code
            else:
                f.write(f"{w:.2f},{intens:.3f}\n")
                
    print(f"         Generated {len(wavelengths)} rows with 3 intentional flaws.")


def load_and_clean_data(filename="spectrometry_raw.csv"):
    """
    Reads CSV file with defensive exception handling, skipping bad records.
    """
    print(f"[Stage 2] Ingesting and sanitizing data from '{filename}'...")
    
    clean_w = []
    clean_i = []
    dropped_count = 0
    
    if not os.path.exists(filename):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Required data file '{filename}' was not found.")
        
    with open(filename, "r") as f:
        for line_num, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
            line_str = line.strip()
            
            # Skip comments and header
            if line_str.startswith("#") or "Wavelength" in line_str or not line_str:
                continue
                
            parts = line_str.split(",")
            try:
                if len(parts) != 2:
                    raise IndexError(f"Expected 2 columns, found {len(parts)}")
                    
                w_val = float(parts[0])
                i_val = float(parts[1])
                
                # Check physical validity (negative readings indicate hardware error)
                if i_val < 0 or w_val <= 0:
                    raise ValueError(f"Physically invalid measurement: ({w_val}, {i_val})")
                    
                clean_w.append(w_val)
                clean_i.append(i_val)
                
            except (ValueError, IndexError) as err:
                dropped_count += 1
                # In production code, log the error rather than crashing
                # print(f"         Skipping row {line_num}: {err}")
                
    print(f"         Successfully parsed {len(clean_w)} valid rows (Filtered out {dropped_count} bad rows).")
    return np.array(clean_w), np.array(clean_i)


def analyze_spectrum(wavelengths, intensities):
    """Computes spectral features, peak wavelengths, and background."""
    print("[Stage 3] Running NumPy numerical processing...")
    
    # 1. Baseline estimation using linear fit on edges
    left_mask = wavelengths < 430.0
    right_mask = wavelengths > 680.0
    edge_w = np.concatenate([wavelengths[left_mask], wavelengths[right_mask]])
    edge_i = np.concatenate([intensities[left_mask], intensities[right_mask]])
    
    # Fit line: y = m*x + b
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(edge_w, edge_i, deg=1)
    baseline = slope * wavelengths + intercept
    
    # 2. Baseline subtraction
    corrected_intensity = intensities - baseline
    
    # 3. Peak Identification
    peak_idx = np.argmax(corrected_intensity)
    peak_w = wavelengths[peak_idx]
    peak_max_counts = corrected_intensity[peak_idx]
    
    # 4. Integrated Signal Area (Trapezoidal Rule)
    total_area = np.trapezoid(np.maximum(corrected_intensity, 0), wavelengths)
    
    results = {
        "baseline": baseline,
        "corrected": corrected_intensity,
        "peak_wavelength": peak_w,
        "peak_intensity": peak_max_counts,
        "integrated_area": total_area,
        "mean_noise_std": np.std(edge_i - (slope * edge_w + intercept))
    }
    return results


def generate_visual_and_text_report(w, i_raw, analysis, 
                                    fig_name="spectrometry_analysis.png", 
                                    report_name="spectrometry_report.txt"):
    """Creates a publication plot and formats an executive summary."""
    print("[Stage 4] Producing output visualizations and executive report...")
    
    # --- Part A: 3-Panel Matplotlib Figure ---
    fig, (ax1, ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(9, 10), sharex=True)
    fig.suptitle("Spectrometry Acquisition & Diagnostic Analysis", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    
    # Subplot 1: Raw Signal and Baseline
    ax1.plot(w, i_raw, "b.", markersize=3, label="Raw Sensor Readings")
    ax1.plot(w, analysis["baseline"], "r--", linewidth=1.8, label="Estimated Linear Baseline")
    ax1.set(ylabel="Intensity (counts)", title="Raw Spectral Profile & Baseline")
    ax1.legend(loc="upper left")
    ax1.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
    
    # Subplot 2: Corrected Signal & Peak Marker
    corr = analysis["corrected"]
    ax2.plot(w, corr, "darkgreen", linewidth=1.5, label="Baseline-Corrected Signal")
    ax2.plot(analysis["peak_wavelength"], analysis["peak_intensity"], "r*", markersize=14, 
             label=f"Dominant Peak: {analysis['peak_wavelength']:.1f} nm")
    ax2.fill_between(w, 0, np.maximum(corr, 0), color="green", alpha=0.15, label="Integrated Band")
    ax2.set(ylabel="Corrected (counts)", title="Baseline-Corrected Emission Peaks")
    ax2.legend(loc="upper left")
    ax2.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
    
    # Subplot 3: Residual Edge Noise
    residuals = i_raw - analysis["baseline"]
    ax3.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle="--")
    ax3.plot(w, residuals, color="gray", linewidth=1.0, label="Noise Residuals")
    ax3.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Residuals", title="Sensor Noise Floor")
    ax3.legend(loc="upper left")
    ax3.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
    
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(fig_name, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    print(f"         Saved figure: '{fig_name}'")
    plt.show()
    
    # --- Part B: Executive Text Summary ---
    with open(report_name, "w") as f:
        f.write("=" * 65 + "\n")
        f.write("      EXECUTIVE SPECTROMETRY ANALYSIS SUMMARY REPORT\n")
        f.write("=" * 65 + "\n")
        f.write(f"Wavelength Range Monitored:   [{w[0]:.1f} nm - {w[-1]:.1f} nm]\n")
        f.write(f"Valid Samples Processed:      {len(w):d}\n")
        f.write(f"Estimated Noise Floor (Std):  {analysis['mean_noise_std']:.3f} counts\n")
        f.write("-" * 65 + "\n")
        f.write("IDENTIFIED SPECTRAL FEATURES:\n")
        f.write(f"  * Dominant Emission Peak:   {analysis['peak_wavelength']:8.2f} nm\n")
        f.write(f"  * Peak Signal Height:       {analysis['peak_intensity']:8.2f} counts\n")
        f.write(f"  * Total Integrated Power:   {analysis['integrated_area']:8.2f} counts*nm\n")
        f.write("=" * 65 + "\n")
        f.write("STATUS: Pipeline executed with ZERO unhandled exceptions.\n")
        
    print(f"         Saved summary: '{report_name}'")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Execute full pipeline end-to-end
    raw_file = "spectrometry_raw.csv"
    generate_mock_laboratory_file(raw_file)
    w_clean, i_clean = load_and_clean_data(raw_file)
    spectral_metrics = analyze_spectrum(w_clean, i_clean)
    generate_visual_and_text_report(w_clean, i_clean, spectral_metrics)
    print("\n[SUCCESS] Capstone analysis pipeline completed successfully!")

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
section: 1. IndexError: list index out of range
text:
1. IndexError: list index out of range

What happened: You tried to access an element at an index that doesn’t exist (e.g., accessing index 5 in a 3-element list).
Remember: In Python, indices run from 0 to len(list) - 1.
Fix: Check len(my_list) before indexing, or use for item in my_list: instead of index loops.

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
section: 2. TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str
text:
2. TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str

What happened: You tried to add a number to text with + (e.g. "Temp: " + 23.5).
Fix: Use an f-string: f"Temp: {23.5}" or convert with str(23.5).

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
section: 3. ValueError: could not convert string to float: '...'
text:
3. ValueError: could not convert string to float: '...'

What happened: You passed non-numeric text to float() (e.g. float("N/A") or an unstripped header line from a file).
Fix: Clean and strip the string, or wrap the conversion in a try...except ValueError block.

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
text:
4. NameError: name 'np' is not defined

What happened: You used a variable or imported library before defining or importing it.
Fix: Ensure import numpy as np is at the very top of your file.

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
text:
5. IndentationError: expected an indented block

What happened: Python requires 4 spaces for indented blocks after def, for, if, or try:.
Fix: Select the affected lines in Spyder and press Tab (or Shift + Tab to unindent). Avoid mixing tabs and spaces.

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
section: 6. ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3,)
text:
6. ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3,)

What happened: In NumPy, you tried to perform an elementwise operation (like a + b or a * b) on two arrays with incompatible shapes.
Fix: Check a.shape and b.shape in Spyder’s Variable Explorer to ensure their dimensions align.

title: Appendix E: Common Error Messages and Fixes
text:
7. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '...'

What happened: Python cannot find the .py file you tried to import.
Fix: In Spyder, check your working directory (top-right folder path) and ensure it points to the folder containing your module.

Appendix F: Managing Packages with Conda and Pip
While Anaconda comes pre-installed with over 200 scientific packages, you may eventually need to install specialized libraries (such as scikit-learn, sympy, or pandas).

title: Appendix F: Managing Packages with Conda and Pip
text:
1. Conda vs Pip

conda: The package manager built into Anaconda. It handles both Python packages and low-level C/Fortran binary dependencies (essential for scientific libraries).
pip: The standard Python package installer. Use pip only if a package is unavailable via conda.

title: Appendix F: Managing Packages with Conda and Pip
text:
2. Essential Conda Commands
Run these commands in your Anaconda Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (macOS/Linux):
# 1. Search for a package
conda search scipy

# 2. Install a package in your active environment
conda install scipy -y

# 3. Install a package from conda-forge (community channel)
conda install -c conda-forge sympy -y

# 4. List all installed packages and their versions
conda list

# 5. Update a package to the latest release
conda update numpy -y

# 6. Remove an unwanted package
conda remove package_name
